facts.statement: The study used a fear conditioning setup with two different locations to test male mice.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: Researchers found a specific state of slow breathing and stillness that happens when mice are in safe areas after avoiding a threat.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: This recovery state involves breathing at a rate of 2 to 4 times per second and the hippocampus replaying the scary memory during specific brain waves.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: How stressed the mice were after the task depended on the mix of time spent freezing versus time in the slow-breathing state, not on how many shocks they got.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: Blocking the specific brain waves in the hippocampus made the slow-breathing state happen less often and made the mice more stressed.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: Giving the drug diazepam increased the slow-breathing state while blocking the brain waves, showing that the physical relief is separate from the hippocampus's role.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: The results suggest that the hippocampus replaying memories helps the body recover and build emotional resilience.
facts.subject: animals
